newsitem.title: GERMANY: German parties edge closer to budget accord.
newsitem.headline: German parties edge closer to budget accord.

text.p: Germany's squabbling coalition partners said on Tuesday they were moving closer to an agreement on the divisive question of how to reduce the country's budget deficit in order to qualify for Europe's single currency.

The issue -- revolving around whether to raise taxes -- has driven a wedge between government allies and weakened Chancellor Helmut Kohl's standing as a long-stifled debate on the euro currency began to erupt in Germany.

Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) have held a series of meetings with its pro-business Free Democrat (FDP) partners aimed at plugging the budget holes and resolving the most serious crisis to face the coalition in its 14-year history.

"We are not at the end of the talks, but we moving in the right direction and it could happen fast," said Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of the FDP, adding a deal could be completed before July.
The coalition will meet in Bonn on Wednesday and will dicuss deficit-cutting suggestions such as accelerating the pace of privatisations, cutting spending and raising new borrowing.
"The budget consolidation will succeed without tax increases," Westerwelle added.

Wolfgang Schaeuble, the CDU's parliamentary group leader, said the coalition agreed on the goal of cutting tax rates, but said there was also a broad consensus that the government could not afford to ignore the possibility of lower tax revenues -- a coded signal that the CDU refuses to rule out tax increases.

Failure to cut the deficit has reduced the chances that Germany will meet fiscal requirements for European economic and monetary union. The Maastricht Treaty permits budget deficits of no more than three percent of gross domestic product.
Otto Lambsdorff, a former economics minister and honourary FDP chairman, said Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Waigel should face up to the fact Germany will not fulfil the Maastricht criteria in 1997.

"One day the finance minister is going to have to back down from his position of 3.0 percent," Lambsdorff said, referring to Waigel's view that Germany must keep its deficit at or below that level in order to qualify for currency union.
"I have always thought it was odd from an economics point of view to cling firmly to that number."

Lambsdorff, joining a chorus of coalition figures urging Waigel to take a relaxed view on the criteria for EMU, said that the euro should move ahead as long as Germany can limit its deficit to 3.3 percent of GDP or less.
Some newspapers on Tuesday still portrayed the government partners as no nearer to solving an issue which has strained the coalition for months.
"It is still far from clear how they will get out of this big mess," Handelsblatt daily wrote in an editorial.

"Running about like a bunch of chickens with their heads cut off, coalition leaders are cackling over high debts, fast privatisations, cutbacks and higher taxes. The government is grabbing at straws."
The opposition Social Democrats, gaining in popularity and reluctant to assist Kohl's 14-year-old government out of the jam, turned up the volume on its calls for early elections.
Gerhard Schroeder, the premier of Lower Saxony who may be the SPD's challenger to Kohl, said the CDU/FDP government had clearly run out of ideas and should resign.
